76	### 1. Define the System Context
77	
78	Every EDF begins by declaring its System Context.
79	
80	System Context has three required fields:
81	
82	- Primary System
83	- Context
84	- Focus
85	
86	These define what is being analyzed, what larger system materially influences it, and what aspect of the primary system is under examination.
87	
88	Different analyses may disagree partly because they declared different System Contexts. That is not automatically a conflict in evidence.

91	
92	State the outcome in factual terms, not interpretive terms.
93	
94	Good:
95	
96	- Two aircraft were lost and the fleet was grounded
97	- The mission landed on the moon and returned safely
98

100

105

107

228	CASE OD2-DEV-MISLEAD: Checkout payment failures after the v4.12 release
229	
230	Setting: Fernhollow Outfitters is a fictional online outdoor-gear retailer. Its checkout service, checkout-api (16 pods), sends card payments to an external gateway, Quillmark Payments, using API credentials. Since 3 March, roughly one payment attempt in 27 has failed, and the failures come and go. A new checkout release (v4.12) went out that morning, and a spring promotion started the same day. Engineering wants to roll the release back, and Finance wants a revenue-impact figure for the board.
231	
232	Presenting request: The Head of Engineering asks: what is causing the intermittent payment failures since 3 March, should we approve the full rollback of checkout-api v4.12, and what should we do now?
233	
234	INITIAL EVIDENCE
235	E1 [stage S1] Incident ticket INC-4471, checkout on-call (system-record): INC-4471 opened 3 March 11:20 by paging alert checkout_payment_failure_rate (rule: 30-minute failure rate at least 2% AND at least 40 failed attempts). Daily payment-attempt failure rate, checkout-api: 28 Feb 0.4%, 1 Mar 0.4%, 2 Mar 0.5%, 3 Mar 3.4%, 4 Mar 3.9%, 5 Mar 3.6%, 6 Mar 3.8%. All new failures carry error code PAYMENT_UPSTREAM_REJECTED. On-call summary: 'Intermittent. A customer fails, retries a few minutes later, often succeeds.' No pod restarts and no gateway timeouts recorded.
236	E2 [stage S1] Email from Dara Okonjo, Engineering Manager, Checkout, 6 March (manager-account): Subject: INC-4471, we know what this is. v4.12 shipped 3 March at 10:40 and the alert fired forty minutes later. The failure rate went from half a percent to nearly four overnight and has stayed there. v4.12 replaced our gateway HTTP client and connection-pool settings, which is exactly the code path that's failing. Quillmark's status page is green, so it isn't them. I want approval to roll the whole fleet back to v4.11 tonight and freeze checkout releases until we've rewritten the client. Dara
237	E3 [stage S1] Release notes, checkout-api v4.12 (CHG-2214) (change-record): checkout-api v4.12, deployed 3 March 10:40, CHG-2214, approved by Engineering CAB. Changes: (1) Gateway client moved to a new HTTP library; connection pool size raised from 50 to 64. (2) Error handling: every non-2xx response from the payment gateway now maps to one code, PAYMENT_UPSTREAM_REJECTED. The raw upstream status is no longer logged at INFO level. The customer message is unchanged: 'Your card was declined. Please try another card or try again.' (3) Security: partial card numbers previously written to debug logs are now masked, closing audit finding SEC-2291 (remediation deadline 13 March). A rollback to v4.11 reverts all three changes.
238	E4 [stage S1] Quillmark Payments status page capture and support ticket TS-90412 (vendor-account): Quillmark status page, captured 6 March 08:00: 'All systems operational' for Authorisation API, Search API and Merchant Dashboard on every day from 1 to 6 March; no incidents posted. Support ticket TS-90412, Quillmark reply of 5 March: 'We see no platform-wide incidents during the period. Our records show your requests are reaching us. Please review your integration and confirm you are handling all documented response codes.'
239	E5 [stage S1] Email from Priya Halvorsen, CFO, 6 March (leadership-account): Gross online revenue for the week to 6 March is down 9% on the prior week. The prior week did include the final days of Winter Clearance, which ended 1 March, and Spring Trail Sale launched on 3 March, but I'm clear in my mind that the checkout failures are what cost us. I need a figure for the board pack on Monday, and I expect us to restate the Q1 forecast on the back of it.
240	E6 [stage S1] Customer Care lead Tomasz Reyes, notes for INC-4471 bridge call, 5 March (staff-account): 238 customer contacts since 3 March about declined cards. Most say the decline came 'out of nowhere' and that a retry a few minutes later worked. Eleven customers phoned their bank. In nine of those cases the bank said it had no record of any authorisation attempt at the time of the failure. Agents have been advising customers to try a different card.
241	
242	EVIDENCE CATALOGUE (collect at most 5; read the file path to collect)
243	X1 [stage S1] Quillmark API usage report for credential fernhollow-prod-01, 1–6 March - source: Quillmark account team (vendor-account) - file: evidence/X1.txt
244	X2 [stage S1] Per-minute payment failure counts, 3–6 March - source: Checkout analytics (telemetry) - file: evidence/X2.txt
245	X3 [stage S1] Sample of 50 Customer Care tickets, 3–6 March - source: Customer Care (customer-account) - file: evidence/X3.txt
246	X4 [stage S1] checkout-api pod resource and connection-pool metrics, 1–6 March - source: Platform monitoring (telemetry) - file: evidence/X4.txt
247	X5 [stage S1] 3-D Secure challenge and fraud-screening statistics, 24 Feb–6 March - source: Payments risk team (telemetry) - file: evidence/X5.txt
248	X6 [stage S1] Peer review record for the v4.12 gateway client change (PR #1187) - source: Source control system (document) - file: evidence/X6.txt
249	X7 [stage S1] Gateway TLS certificate, DNS and egress firewall change history, January–March - source: Platform team (change-record) - file: evidence/X7.txt
250	X8 [stage S1] Interview with the engineer who built the v4.12 gateway client - source: Interview notes, Sana Oyelaran, senior engineer, 6 March (staff-account) - file: evidence/X8.txt
251	X9 [stage S1] Finance Systems change log, February–March - source: Finance Systems team (change-record) - file: evidence/X9.txt
252	X10 [stage S1] Canary rollback test results, CHG-2231, 5 March 12:00–18:00 - source: Checkout platform team (change-record) - file: evidence/X10.txt
253	X11 [stage S1] Internal audit finding SEC-2291 and remediation correspondence - source: Internal Audit (document) - file: evidence/X11.txt
254	X12 [stage S1] Marketing performance report, Spring Trail Sale, 3–6 March - source: Digital marketing team (document) - file: evidence/X12.txt
255	
256	CANDIDATE HYPOTHESES
257	H1: A defect in checkout-api v4.12 (the new gateway HTTP client or its connection-pool settings) is causing the rise in payment failures.
258	H2: Quillmark is throttling Fernhollow's shared gateway credential because the finance settlement-reconciliation job's quarter-hourly search bursts push it over its per-credential rate limit, and checkout payment calls are rejected as a result.
259	H3: A real rise in card issuers declining payments (for example tighter issuer fraud rules) is driving the rise in failures.
260	H4: A platform-wide degradation at Quillmark, affecting its merchants generally, is causing the failures.
261	
262	CANDIDATE CAUSAL LINKS
263	R1: Deployment of checkout-api v4.12 on 3 March at 10:40 -> Rise in checkout payment failure rate from about 0.4% to about 3.7% (causes)
264	R2: settle-recon moved to a 15-minute daytime schedule on the shared credential fernhollow-prod-01 (FIN-CHG-0187) -> Quillmark returning HTTP 429 rate-limit responses to fernhollow-prod-01 (causes)
265	R3: Quillmark returning HTTP 429 rate-limit responses to fernhollow-prod-01 -> Customers seeing 'card declined' failures at checkout (causes)
266	R4: Rise in checkout payment failure rate since 3 March -> 9% week-on-week fall in gross online revenue for the week to 6 March (causes)
267	
268	CANDIDATE ACTIONS
269	A1: Roll the full checkout-api fleet back to v4.11 tonight and freeze checkout releases until the gateway client is rewritten.
270	A2: Revert settle-recon to its nightly schedule (or pause its daytime runs) now, then watch the 429 rate and payment failure rate to confirm recovery, and give the job its own credential before any future daytime schedule.
271	A3: Tell the board the payment incident caused the 9% week-on-week revenue fall and restate the Q1 revenue forecast on that basis.
272	A4: Ask Quillmark for a temporary increase in the rate limit for credential fernhollow-prod-01.

276	Q2: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
277	Q3: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
278	Q4: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
279	Q5: edge R1 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
280	Q6: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
281	Q7: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
282	Q8: edge R4 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]

284	Q10: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
285	Q11: action A3 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
286	Q12: action A4 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]

# EDF Specification v0.3

Status: Working draft

This is the authoritative EDF v0.3 specification for the current draft.

Under EDF's constitutional version integrity rule, this defines a subsequent version rather than changing the meaning of v0.2 retroactively.

EDF evolves under constitutional rules defined in [constitution.md](constitution.md). The constitution governs framework evolution, not how to perform an EDF analysis.

## Purpose

EDF is a systems understanding framework with a diagnostic grammar.

It is used to explain how a system produced an outcome and to identify the highest-leverage opportunities for influencing future outcomes.

EDF is not primarily a decision framework. It establishes confidence in reality before decision frameworks such as Clarity evaluate what to do next.

Diagnostic Calibration is an optional extension for comparing, challenging, refining, and synthesizing multiple EDF analyses of the same system.

Framework changes should remain consistent with the constitutional rules of EDF.

## Design Rule

If a new concept does not improve one of the five verbs, it does not belong in EDF.

The five verbs are:

- Define
- Observe
- Explain
- Influence
- Validate

## Context Principle

Every EDF analysis is valid only within its declared System Context.

## Required Diagnostic Sequence

Every EDF analysis should follow this sequence:

1. Define the System Context
   - Primary System
   - Context
   - Focus
2. Define the Outcome
3. Identify Manifestation(s)
4. Build the Origin Network
5. Trace Propagation
6. Evaluate Evidence
7. Identify Control Points
8. Rank Control Points
9. Determine Diagnostic Sufficiency

## Sequence Notes

### 1. Define the System Context

Every EDF begins by declaring its System Context.

System Context has three required fields:

- Primary System
- Context
- Focus

These define what is being analyzed, what larger system materially influences it, and what aspect of the primary system is under examination.

Different analyses may disagree partly because they declared different System Contexts. That is not automatically a conflict in evidence.

### 2. Define the Outcome

State the outcome in factual terms, not interpretive terms.

Good:

- Two aircraft were lost and the fleet was grounded
- The mission landed on the moon and returned safely

Weak:

- Management failed
- The launch culture was broken

### 3. Identify Manifestation(s)

Manifestations are observable signals.

They are how the outcome appears in the world. A complex outcome may have several manifestations.

### 4. Build the Origin Network

Identify the contributing origins that made the outcome possible.

Origins may be:

- Technical
- Human
- Organizational
- Environmental
- Financial
- Regulatory

Complex outcomes should usually be modeled as an origin network rather than a single root cause.

### 5. Trace Propagation

Describe how effects moved from the origin network to the manifestations and outcome.

Propagation paths may be:

- Physical
- Informational
- Organizational
- Financial
- Human

### 6. Evaluate Evidence

Separate direct observation from inference.

Evaluate the quality of evidence supporting the current model and note meaningful gaps or disputes.

### 7. Identify Control Points

Identify where intervention could most effectively influence future outcomes.

Control points may differ from origins.

### 8. Rank Control Points

Rank candidate control points using:

- Influence
- Controllability
- Cost
- Confidence

The ranking does not need false precision. It does need a defensible ordering.

### 9. Determine Diagnostic Sufficiency

Ask:

> Do we understand enough to take the next responsible action?

Diagnosis is sufficient when additional investigation is unlikely to materially change the next responsible action.

## Required Output Elements

All EDF outputs should include, at minimum:

- System Context
- Primary System
- Context
- Focus
- Outcome
- Manifestation(s)
- Origin Network
- Propagation
- Evidence
- Control Points
- Control Point Ranking
- Confidence
- Diagnostic Sufficiency
- Unknowns
- Next Responsible Action

## Optional Extension: Diagnostic Calibration

Diagnostic Calibration is not required for routine EDF use.

Use it when:

- The situation is complex
- The stakes are high
- Causes are disputed
- Multiple disciplines are involved
- The cost of being wrong is significant

Diagnostic Calibration uses multiple independent EDF analyses to improve confidence in the diagnostic model while preserving valuable disciplinary perspectives.

See [diagnostic-calibration.md](diagnostic-calibration.md).

## Relationship To Complexity Levels

- Use [EDF-0](complexity-levels.md#edf-0-rapid) for rapid, low-complexity situations.
- Use [EDF-1](complexity-levels.md#edf-1-standard) when evidence and alternatives matter.
- Use [EDF-2](complexity-levels.md#edf-2-complex) when multiple interacting origins and layered control points must be modeled.

The sequence remains the same across levels. The depth changes.

## Relationship To Clarity

EDF creates the diagnostic grammar.

Diagnostic Calibration improves confidence in the diagnostic model.

Clarity uses the calibrated understanding to evaluate decisions.

## Additional decision rules for this analysis

1. Treat the presenting request as one hypothesis, not a fact. Keep its rivals live until evidence rules them out: no real problem (normal variation or a baseline explains it); an intentional tradeoff; an outside cause; a measurement or reporting artifact; a cause in a different unit or component from the one blamed.
2. Judge every action by what it would do under every live hypothesis, not only the leading one. An action is harmful if it is likely to cause damage even when the leading hypothesis is true: punishing the messenger or the wrong party, suppressing information, rewarding a gamed metric, or disabling a protective control. An action is premature if it is only sensible when a still-unconfirmed hypothesis is true.
3. "No intervention is warranted" is a valid, sufficient conclusion when the evidence shows the problem does not exist or is an accepted tradeoff.
4. Evidence collection is governed by value of information. Before each collection, name the live hypotheses and the answer or action that is most uncertain. Collect an item only if its title suggests it could discriminate between live hypotheses or change your next action. Stop as soon as no remaining item could change your next action. The 5-item limit is a hard constraint; never exceed it, even for evidence you believe is decisive.

input.brief: The failures are most likely caused by Finance's settlement-reconciliation job, not release v4.12. On 3 March it moved from a nightly run to every 15 minutes during the day. It shares one Quillmark credential with checkout. Each run sends bursts of 360–430 requests a minute against a 300-per-minute limit. Quillmark answers with HTTP 429 (too many requests), and checkout shows that as "card declined". The canary test settles the v4.12 question. Pods on the old v4.11 failed at 3.7% and pods on v4.12 at 3.6%. Almost all of the old-version failures were 429s. Issuer declines stayed flat, and Quillmark has no platform incident. A full rollback would not fix this. It would also undo the card-number masking required by SEC-2291, which is due 13 March. Next steps: (1) pause or revert the daytime settle-recon schedule now, then watch the 429 rate and the payment failure rate; (2) give that job its own credential before any daytime schedule returns; (3) change checkout to log the real gateway status and to retry or handle 429s; (4) don't attribute the 9% revenue drop to the incident yet. Traffic, conversion and order value changed with the sale, and the failed customers often succeeded on retry. A rate-limit increase is slow and chargeable, so keep it as a backup. I'm fairly confident, around 85–90%.
